strengths: Strong empirical results across multiple large-scale datasets (QM9, GEOM-Drugs, B3LYP), with particularly impressive 99.0% validity and 24.2% molecule stability on B3LYP
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including unconditional and class-conditional generation with multiple chemical validity metrics
Sound technical approach combining inertial frame canonicalization for SE(3) invariance with GeoRoPE for geometry-aware attention
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and formal theoretical grounding (Theorem 1)
Extensive supplementary material with detailed proofs and technical exposition
Practical contributions to important problem of 3D molecule generation with demonstrated controllability (83.3% hit rate)
weaknesses: Limited individual technical novelty - inertial frame canonicalization, RoPE-3D, diffusion loss, and classifier-free guidance are all existing techniques; contribution is primarily in their combination

Critical absence of ablation studies on key design choices: no ablation on inertial frame canonicalization, GeoRoPE components separately, hierarchical vs. joint prediction, or block-diagonal structure in attention

Baseline comparison fairness concerns: B3LYP results only compare against EDM and Geo2Seq (others excluded due to 'computational cost'), and Geo2Seq's 73.3% validity vs. InertialAR's 99.0% gap suggests potential implementation issues

Unexplained empirical phenomena: molecule stability metric varies dramatically across datasets (24.2% on B3LYP vs. 0.8% for EDM, but 94.7% vs. 89.4% on QM9), with no discussion of why or whether metrics are consistently computed

Insufficient technical justification for design choices: claim that 'RoPE-3D alone cannot learn adequate information' is unsupported empirical observation; fourth-node selection criteria (largest distance, first quadrant placement) appear arbitrary
Missing analysis of failure modes, edge cases, and scalability: no discussion of symmetric molecules with degenerate eigenvalues, no failure case analysis, no scalability study vs. molecule size
No computational cost analysis: training time, inference time, and memory requirements not reported; anchor point selection for Nystrom approximation not detailed
Insufficient differentiation from concurrent work using inertial frames (Guo et al. 2025, Lu et al. 2025a/b, Cheng et al. 2025b)
Metric reporting inconsistency: abstract claims '7 of 10' SOTA metrics but tables show 8/12 across datasets
Limited reproducibility details: hyperparameter sensitivity not discussed, code availability not mentioned, functional group detection pipeline's 3D→2D→patterns conversion is lossy and error-prone

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing fundamental challenges in extending AR models to 3D molecule generation
Comprehensive technical approach systematically addressing SE(3) invariance, tokenization, and architecture design
Strong empirical results on multiple datasets (QM9, GEOM-Drugs, B3LYP) with state-of-the-art performance on many metrics
Extensive mathematical exposition with detailed appendices including proofs and theoretical justification
Demonstrates effectiveness on both unconditional and class-conditional generation tasks
Good experimental scope covering multiple evaluation settings and datasets
weaknesses: Critical absence of ablation studies in main paper or appendices—impossible to validate necessity of three major components (inertial frames, GeoRoPE, hierarchical AR) or understand contribution of each

Unjustified design choices: (1) Diffusion loss for coordinates lacks any empirical validation—paper only states 'regression yields poor performance' with no supporting evidence, (2) GeoRoPE complexity unjustified—claim that RoPE-3D alone is insufficient is unsupported and unmeasured
Misleading claims about results: abstract claims 'state-of-the-art on 7 of 10 metrics' but Table 1 shows only 4 metrics; discrepancy unexplained, damaging credibility

Inertial frame canonicalization has unaddressed issues: degenerate eigenvalues for symmetric molecules create non-unique frames, fourth-node approach is ad-hoc without robustness analysis, RDKit ordering choice for AR not justified
No computational efficiency validation despite efficiency claims—missing timing comparisons, memory analysis, and cost breakdown of Nyström approximation and diffusion loss inference

Limited error analysis: no failure mode characterization, no qualitative analysis of generated structures, no sensitivity analysis to hyperparameters (e.g., Nyström anchor points), no investigation of performance on different molecule types
Marginal improvements over baselines in many cases (QM9 AtomSta: 99.3% vs 99.0%; Validity: 97.4% vs 97.1%) without explanation of significance
Incomplete reproducibility information: Nyström anchor points m unspecified, B3LYP training details sparse, hyperparameter choices for diffusion loss underspecified, no code mentioned
Terminology imprecision: describes achieving 'SE(3) equivariance' when the approach achieves SE(3) invariance through canonicalization—these are distinct concepts
Limited scope of conditional generation evaluation: only 5 of many functional group classes tested, no analysis on less frequent classes

strengths: Novel canonical tokenization using inertial frames with formal proof for axis direction uniqueness, elegantly addressing SE(3) invariance requirement
Creative GeoRoPE architecture combining RoPE-3D with Nystrom approximation encoding for geometry-aware attention, with clear mathematical formulation (Eq. 14)
Strong empirical results across three diverse datasets, particularly impressive controllable generation (83.3% hit rate) and B3LYP molecule stability (24.2% vs 0.8% for EDM)
Comprehensive experimental validation including unconditional and conditional generation with reasonable baselines (Geo2Seq, UniGEM, EDM)
Practical advantages: single forward pass generation + better controllability via classifier-free guidance compared to iterative diffusion methods
Clear presentation with well-organized narrative, effective figures, and detailed mathematical appendices
weaknesses: Theoretical terminology imprecise: paper claims 'SE(3)-equivariance' but achieves SE(3)-invariance; no formal proof that entire tokenization pipeline is invariant, only the inertial frame construction

Critical lack of ablation studies: paper states RoPE-3D alone is insufficient empirically but provides no quantitative evidence or ablation table; no separate evaluation of RoPE-3D vs Nystrom components
Insufficient comparison on B3LYP: only two baselines (EDM and Geo2Seq) evaluated; computational cost justifiable but limits confidence in relative performance claims
Unvalidated efficiency claims: paper advertises 'highly efficient generation' but provides no timing comparisons, denoising step counts, or computational complexity analysis
Missing reproducibility details: number of Nystrom anchor points, RBF width σ, diffusion noise schedule, denoising steps, training hyperparameters not specified; no code availability mentioned

Molecular validity concerns: coordinates generated without explicit bond constraints; no discussion of how Nystrom distance encoding ensures reasonable bond lengths or whether generated structures require geometry optimization
No statistical significance testing: results appear to be single runs without error bars or confidence intervals; some improvements (e.g., 99.3% vs 99.0%) within noise margins
Heavy RDKit dependency for canonical reordering without discussion of robustness to edge cases or failure modes; reliance on external library heuristics introduces potential fragility

Limited justification for design choices: block-diagonal weight matrices (Eq. 12) appear ad-hoc; no exploration of alternative continuous distribution approaches to diffusion loss; hierarchical vs joint prediction not ablated

strengths: Strong empirical results, particularly on large-scale B3LYP (99.3% validity vs 92.9% for EDM), demonstrating scalability beyond small molecule benchmarks
Outstanding controllable generation performance (83.3% average hit rate vs 37-40% for baselines), enabling practical molecular editing
Thorough experimental validation with comprehensive ablation studies (Tables 6-7) and robustness analysis (Section E.1) showing inertial frames are empirically stable
Rigorous theoretical justification with formal Theorem D.1 and proof for the fourth anchor point strategy
Well-motivated hierarchical architecture sensibly decoupling discrete atom types and continuous 3D coordinates via Diffusion Loss, with ablation showing dramatic degradation with L2 regression
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figure 1 overview, Figure 4 molecule editing) and thorough mathematical exposition
Practical contributions enabling efficient variable-length generation and controllable inference via classifier-free guidance
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty: primarily combines inertial frame canonicalization (concurrent works Guo et al. 2025, Lu et al. 2025a), standard RDKit reordering, and existing Diffusion Loss (Li et al. 2024a) with incremental improvements

Modest improvements over Geo2Seq on standard benchmarks (QM9: 97.3% vs 97.1% validity; only substantial gain in MolSta at 94.5% vs 93.2%), limiting evidence of practical advantages on smaller datasets

Insufficient ablation studies: missing justification for Manhattan+Euclidean PE concatenation, block-diagonal weight structure (Eq. 12), Nyström vs alternative approximations, and CFG applied to both type/coordinate predictions

Theoretical concerns with SE(3)-invariance claim: method only achieves invariance up to inertial frame choice with residual sign ambiguities; claim that 'our contribution is not theoretically perfect canonicalization' somewhat undermines core premise

strengths: Strong empirical results across multiple datasets (QM9, GEOM-Drugs, B3LYP), particularly for class-conditional generation with 83.3% average hit rate
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple metrics, proper ablations (Sections E.2-E.3), and robustness analyses demonstrating inertial frame stability under perturbations
Well-executed technical integration combining inertial frames, geometric positional encoding, and hierarchical autoregressive prediction in a coherent system
Thorough presentation with clear motivation, informative figures, and detailed experimental setup supporting reproducibility
Addresses a real and underexplored problem in extending autoregressive models to 3D molecular generation
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty: inertial frames (Guo et al. 2025, Lu et al. 2025a), RDKit reordering (standard practice), GeoPE (combines existing techniques Su 2021, Williams & Seeger 2000), Diffusion Loss (Li et al. 2024a), and CFG (Ho & Salimans 2022) are all borrowed; the main claim is applying known techniques to autoregressive generation, which is primarily engineering

Theoretical limitations of canonical tokenization are acknowledged but unresolved: axis ambiguities and discontinuities are addressed ad hoc via a fourth-node trick rather than principled solutions; empirical robustness (0.007% degeneracy) does not validate theoretical soundness

SE(3)-invariance claimed for tokenization but sequential autoregressive generation conditions on previously generated atoms, breaking invariance guarantees during generation—this subtle issue is not addressed

Permutation invariance via RDKit SMILES depends on 2D graph structure not 3D geometry; ablation (Table 7) shows removing canonicalization only degrades performance by ~0.4%, questioning its importance
Modest improvements on standard benchmarks: QM9 Valid improves 0.2% (97.3% vs 97.1%), MolSta improves 1.3% (94.5% vs 93.2%); improvements are primarily on Valid&Unique metric

Unfair comparisons on B3LYP: only compared to EDM and Geo2Seq (poor performance: 73.3% valid, 2.7% valid&unique suggests inadequate tuning), prohibitive cost justification excludes other recent methods, weakening SOTA claims

Critical ablations missing: no separate contribution analysis for ManhattanPE vs EuclideanPE, no sensitivity to Nyström anchor points, no justification for factorization choice (p(t|h)·p(c|t,h) vs alternatives), no analysis of why L2 regression completely fails

Inference efficiency entirely ignored: autoregressive sequential generation is inherently slow compared to diffusion models, but no generation speed comparison, sampling efficiency analysis, or deployment considerations provided despite claiming 'highly efficient' generation

Geometric positional encoding motivation unclear: why ManhattanPE specifically helps 3D molecules is not explained; standard 3D positional encodings from literature not considered; GeoPE addition of Euclidean distances justified only empirically ('we empirically observe')
Functional group detection for class-conditional generation uses SMARTS-matching without reliability analysis, error cases, or validation of hit rate metric trustworthiness

strengths: Strong empirical results achieving state-of-the-art on 8/10 metrics across QM9/GEOM-Drugs and all 4 metrics on B3LYP, with particularly impressive molecule stability gains (24.7% vs 0.8% for EDM)

Well-motivated technical approach with sound mathematical foundations, including formal proof for sign disambiguation (Theorem D.1) and thorough empirical robustness analysis showing principle-moment degeneracy affects only 0.007% of QM9
Novel application of inertial frame canonicalization to autoregressive tokenization, credibly claimed as the first work combining these for 3D generation

Comprehensive evaluation across three diverse datasets with 10+ metrics, comparison to 8-10 strong baselines, and meaningful ablations validating design choices (e.g., Diffusion Loss vs L2 regression: 97.4% vs 24.7% validity)
Practical controllability demonstrated through class-conditional generation with 83.3% average hit rate and effective molecule editing via classifier-free guidance
Clear presentation with well-organized content, effective figures, comprehensive appendix, and honest discussion of limitations
weaknesses: Critical missing details on inference efficiency: number of diffusion denoising steps for coordinates not specified, undermining claims about AR efficiency vs diffusion; no sampling speed/latency comparisons despite efficiency being a key motivation

Theoretical canonicalization limitations acknowledged but resolved only pragmatically: PCA has known issues with axis flips and degenerate eigenvalues; while empirical validation is convincing, this approach lacks strong theoretical guarantees

Limited novelty of individual components: inertial frames, positional encoding, Diffusion Loss, and classifier-free guidance are all existing techniques; contribution is primarily their combination rather than novel methodology

RDKit dependency creates brittleness in atom reordering without discussion of failure modes or comparison to alternative orderings (e.g., atomic number, distance-based), leaving unclear whether SMILES-based ordering is optimal for AR

GeoPE design partially unjustified: no ablation on why Manhattan+Euclidean PE over alternatives, block-diagonal projection justified only as 'maintaining distinct roles' without explaining why independence is preferable to joint modeling, Nyström anchor points (m) not analyzed for sensitivity
B3LYP evaluation limited to only 2 baselines (EDM, Geo2Seq) due to computational constraints, weakening generalization claims despite dramatic improvements

Incomplete reproducibility: model architecture sizes, learning rates, diffusion inference steps, Nyström anchor selection strategy, and training time all missing; code availability claimed but URL not provided
Hierarchical factorization (Eq. 16) lacking validation: no ablation comparing joint vs factorized type-coordinate modeling to justify the independence assumption
No statistical significance testing, error bars, or confidence intervals; inconsistent metric emphasis (e.g., Valid&Unique 98.0% vs UniGEM 98.4% on GEOM-Drugs not highlighted)
Missing analysis of failure cases, maximum molecule size limits, and generalization beyond QM9/GEOM/B3LYP; no comparison of alternative atom orderings for autoregressive generation
